AI application evals.

Sources and what they establish

Demystifying evals for AI agents ↗

Anthropic Engineering · practitioner article · Anthropic · January 9, 2026

The team builds and evaluates AI products and reports experience with customers. Its useful contribution here is the distinction between tasks, attempts, and graders, plus advice on starting small. This is engineering guidance, not a controlled study showing a universal release threshold.

Evaluation best practices ↗

OpenAI · developer documentation · OpenAI API · accessed October 24, 2026

The model and API provider describes how to define objectives, collect examples, and compare changes. We use those design principles, not its illustrative numerical targets or platform instructions. The page does not establish that any particular score makes your support application ready.

τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains ↗

Shunyu Yao, Noah Shinn, Pedram Razavi, Karthik Narasimhan · research preprint · Sierra / arXiv · June 17, 2024, version 1

The authors built the simulated retail and airline environments they evaluate, giving them direct access to actions, database changes, and failures. Their experiments demonstrate a way to measure support tasks and repeated-run reliability. The 2024 model scores are historical, not estimates of today’s models or your customers. Simulated users and simplified policies limit transfer to real deployments.

7.2.4.1. Confidence intervals ↗

NIST/SEMATECH · statistical handbook · e-Handbook of Statistical Methods · accessed October 24, 2026

This statistical reference explains uncertainty when estimating a failure proportion from a finite sample. The mathematics still applies to binary test results when its sampling assumptions hold. It cannot tell us whether our support cases represent real traffic, or whether our judgments are correct.

The direct answer

An eval is a repeatable test of whether your AI application does what you need. You give it a defined situation, record what happens, and judge the result against an explicit requirement. Run many such situations to discover failures and compare versions.

You need evals because a successful API call proves that a request completed. It does not prove that the answer follows your refund policy, refers to the right order, or tells the customer the truth. A convincing demonstration answers one narrow question: “Did this example work on this attempt?” A test collection lets you ask a more useful one: “What keeps working, and what breaks when I change the application?”

You can start with Python, a file of support cases, and a knowledgeable human reviewer. You do not need to train a model or learn machine-learning mathematics first.

1. Decide what success means

Consider an assistant receiving “My headphones broke. Can I get my money back?” The text alone is insufficient. Eligibility may depend on the purchase date, product, order ownership, and exceptions in the policy. If your application searches company documents, that search determines which policy the model sees. If it calls a refund API, your code executes the action. Evaluate that whole application path, because an excellent model cannot answer correctly from a wrong order record.

Start with one supported job. For the worked example below, the assistant only explains refund eligibility and the next step; it cannot issue refunds. That gives you a smaller behavior to evaluate before adding actions.

Constructed policy for this example: unopened products qualify for a refund through day 30 after delivery, inclusive. Opened products require a human review. After day 30, the assistant should explain ineligibility under this policy. It must not invent exceptions or say money has been sent. These are invented company rules, not general retail rules.

A good answer to an unopened purchase delivered 20 days ago explains that it qualifies and how to request the refund. “I refunded you” fails, even if it sounds helpful. “No refunds are possible” also fails. Evaluating both directions prevents an assistant that avoids mistakes simply by refusing every request.

When the assistant can take actions

Then success also requires a correct change to real records. A tool is an ordinary function your application lets the model request, such as refund_order(order_id). The model proposes a call; your code runs it and returns the result. A trace is the record of messages, retrieved documents, tool calls, results, and timing. You do not need access to private model reasoning to inspect these observable events.

What does an actual research evaluation observe? This original figure shows a conversation and the database operations behind it.

Notice that the agent reads the reservation before deciding what is allowed. The customer’s reply changes the requested action to cancellation. The final tool result establishes that cancellation occurred; a sentence claiming cancellation would not. This figure illustrates the benchmark design, not a measured success rate.

There is a second requirement: authorization must precede the action. The paper explicitly notes in §3, “Reward,” that its final-state score can miss an action performed without required confirmation. That is why a real refund evaluation should inspect both the resulting refund and any required permission in the trace. A correct final balance alone cannot prove a correct process.

2. Turn a requirement into a test case

A case contains the situation and the expected behavior. An attempt is one execution of that case. The grader decides whether an attempt meets a requirement. A dataset here is simply your collection of cases; a JSON file is enough.

Keep the expected result separate from the input sent to the assistant. Otherwise you would be telling it the answer and testing a different task.

{
  "id": "refund-day-30",
  "category": "boundary",
  "input": {
    "message": "It arrived 30 days ago, still unopened. Can I return it?",
    "days_since_delivery": 30,
    "opened": false
  },
  "expected": {
    "eligibility": "eligible",
    "must_explain": "A refund can be requested under the policy",
    "must_not_claim": "Refund already issued"
  }
}

Day 30 is a boundary case: it tests the precise point where behavior changes. Day 31 should produce a different answer. This catches an assistant that remembers “30 days” but applies the inequality incorrectly. In an action-taking version, add a fixed clock, starting account records, available tools, and required final records.

Here is a proposed first collection. The counts organize initial work; they do not establish statistical reliability.

CasesWhat to varyWhat failure it exposes
8 ordinaryDifferent wording; eligible and ineligible requestsMisunderstanding common requests
6 boundariesDay 29, 30, 31; opened versus unopenedWrong policy interpretation
6 missing factsUnknown delivery date or product conditionGuessing instead of asking
6 difficult requestsPressure for an exception; requests to ignore policyFollowing customer demands over company rules
4 operational failuresOrder lookup unavailable; conflicting policy versionsInventing information when a dependency fails

For a real business, ask a support specialist to replace the invented policy and review expected answers. Use permitted, de-identified examples from actual support work where available. Keep a typical-traffic sample separate from deliberately difficult cases: their scores answer different questions. Anthropic suggests 20–50 simple tasks as an initial collection, not as proof of readiness. Source: “Step 0. Start early.” ↗

3. Grade meaning, actions, and failure severity

A single exact reference sentence is too restrictive for support prose. “You qualify” and “Your unopened item is within the return window” may both be correct. But accepting any answer containing “refund” is too permissive: “Your refund is complete” contains the word while falsely claiming an action.

For this example, have a reviewer answer three separate questions for each attempt:

  1. Policy: Does the eligibility decision follow the supplied rule and known facts? If a required fact is absent, does it ask rather than guess?
  2. Truthfulness: Does the answer avoid invented facts, unsupported exceptions, and claims of actions it did not perform?
  3. Usefulness: Does it explain the applicable reason and a concrete next step in understandable language?

Use pass, fail, or needs_review, plus a short reason pointing to the relevant text. Missing evidence should not silently become a pass. If reviewers disagree, examine the case and policy before assuming the assistant is wrong.

For an assistant with refund tools, code can check exact order IDs, amounts in cents, duplicate refunds, and final database values. A reviewer can still judge whether the explanation is understandable. A model can eventually assist with grading prose, but it is another fallible program: test its judgments against human-labeled good and bad answers first. Source: “Types of graders” and “Step 5.” ↗

In this proposed design, any false “refund completed” statement is a critical failure. Report it separately. Do not average it away with good tone. Similarly, a tool timeout is an application failure category to investigate, not an incorrect policy answer. Keep these labels separate so the next fix targets the right component.

4. Understand what a score means

If 24 of 30 attempts pass every required check, the observed pass rate is 24 ÷ 30 = 80%. That describes those attempts under that policy, application version, and grading method. It does not mean an arbitrary future customer has an 80% chance of success.

Why? First, your cases may overrepresent easy questions or rare attacks. Second, repeated attempts can produce different answers. Third, the grader can be wrong. A useful report therefore includes counts by category, critical failures, uncertain judgments, and individual failure examples alongside the overall fraction.

What happens when the same task is attempted repeatedly? The original research figure below answers two different questions. The horizontal axis is the number of attempts, k; the vertical axis is a percentage.

Dotted pass@k asks whether at least one attempt succeeds. Solid pass^k asks whether all k attempts succeed. More attempts help the first score and make the second criterion harder. In this experiment, the authors report GPT-4o below 25% on passing all eight attempts, despite above 60% average single-attempt success. Those are different reliability questions, not contradictory results. They do not measure current models.

A customer usually experiences one conversation. Do not run ten attempts, select the best reply, and report that as ordinary single-conversation quality unless your deployed application really performs that selection and you evaluate the selector too. For your first collection, three independent runs per case can reveal instability. They are 90 attempts on 30 situations, not 90 distinct situations.

Even zero observed failures has limits

Suppose failures truly occurred in 5% of independent, representative requests. The probability that 30 tests all miss them is 0.9530, about 21%. That arithmetic explains why 30/30 passes is useful evidence but cannot certify near-perfect reliability.

Under independent sampling from a stable population, a one-sided 95% upper confidence bound after zero failures in 30 attempts is approximately 9.5%, calculated as 1 − 0.051/30. This procedure bounds the underlying failure rate with at least 95% coverage over repeated samples; it is not a guarantee for this application. Handpicked examples and repeated variants of the same case do not automatically satisfy the assumptions. Basis: NIST’s binomial interval method. ↗

5. Start with one repeatable Python run

The companion eval_start.py and cases.json implement the small answer-only workflow. They contain six constructed examples to make the format concrete. Extend them with your actual policy and support cases before drawing business conclusions.

  1. Run a dry demonstration: python3 eval_start.py --demo. This writes canned outputs and pending review records to results.json. It makes no model calls and measures no model quality.
  2. Connect your application: create my_assistant.py with answer(payload), returning a string. Pass payload["policy"] and the customer’s input through your normal application path. Then run python3 eval_start.py --adapter my_assistant:answer --output baseline.json.
  3. Review the results: use the three questions above. Replace each pending judgment with a decision and reason. Keep the generated response and expected behavior together for inspection.
  4. Save the version: record model identifier, prompt revision, policy revision, retrieval settings if any, and the application commit. The starter accepts --version as a label; fill it with meaningful identifiers.

The script passes only policy and case input to your assistant. It stores expected behavior after execution for review. It records response time and exceptions, but intentionally computes no quality score before grading. This avoids treating a successful function call as a correct support answer.

If you later add action-taking, replace live payment and order APIs with an isolated test environment. Reset its records before every attempt; otherwise a previous refund can change the next test’s meaning. Run full conversations too: a first reply can be correct while a later confirmation or second request fails.

6. Use failures to decide what to change

First run the unchanged application to establish a baseline, the reference result you will compare against. Inspect failures: did the application retrieve an outdated policy, did the model misread the correct one, did your tool reject a valid request, or did the grader reject an acceptable answer? Each diagnosis implies a different fix.

Then change one thing, such as the policy instruction, and rerun the same cases with the same grading rules. Compare the actual changed cases, not just the totals. In a constructed 30-case comparison, a new version might fix five cases but break three previously passing cases. A gain of two hides three new problems. One may be a critical false refund claim.

Reserve an additional set of cases that you do not use while tuning. This is a held-out set. It helps reveal whether your changes handle the general rule or merely the examples you kept editing against. Once a held-out case becomes part of development, add fresh ones for the next independent check.

For this proposed refund explainer, a sensible initial release rule is: no observed critical false-action claims, no unexplained regressions on required policy cases, and support-owner acceptance of reviewed answers. These are example decision rules, not a universal numeric quality bar. Passing them still calls for supervised use and review of real failures.

After deployment, sample real conversations and track verified resolutions, unnecessary escalations, time to response, and cost per conversation. A lower escalation rate alone can hide unsupported answers; customers can also stop responding without being helped. Turn confirmed failures into new cases, update expectations when policy changes, and rerun before changing models, prompts, retrieval, or tools. Source: “Design your eval process.” ↗

Your first useful deliverable is modest: a written support requirement, a small set of cases, recorded attempts, explicit judgments, and a concrete explanation of each failure. That is enough to start improving the assistant with evidence.
